title: Hardware, Memory & Number Systems
summary: Memory hierarchy and units, binary/octal/decimal/hex conversions, input-output devices, ports and storage media. Number-conversion and memory-unit questions are near-guaranteed marks because they need no theory recall - only method.

subtopics.title: Memory hierarchy, RAM/ROM and cache
subtopics.concept: A computer keeps data in several kinds of memory. The faster a memory is, the smaller and costlier it is. So the machine stacks them like a ladder: tiny and fast at the top, huge and slow at the bottom. Some memory forgets everything at power-off (volatile). The rest keeps its data.

tricks.title: Volatile means Vanishes
tricks.body: Volatile memories vanish when power goes: registers, cache, RAM. Everything you keep files on (ROM, SSD, HDD, pen drive) is non-volatile.

example.q: Which is volatile, ROM or DRAM?
steps: ROM keeps data without power.
DRAM loses data at power-off.

tricks.title: ROM family eraser
tricks.body: PROM is written once. EPROM is erased by UV light. EEPROM is erased electrically. More E's, more electricity.

example.q: How is EPROM erased?
steps: EPROM is the UV member of the family.

tricks.title: Cache position
tricks.body: Any question that says 'memory between the CPU and main memory' points to cache. L1 is inside the core and fastest.

example.q: Which memory sits between the CPU and RAM?
steps: It holds copies of frequently used data.
It is built from SRAM.

mistakes.wrong: Calling ROM volatile.
mistakes.right: ROM keeps its data without power. It is non-volatile.

mistakes.wrong: Saying SRAM needs refreshing.
mistakes.right: DRAM needs refreshing because its capacitors leak. SRAM does not.

mistakes.wrong: Using SRAM for main memory and DRAM for cache.
mistakes.right: Cache uses fast, costly SRAM. Main memory uses cheaper DRAM.

mistakes.wrong: Treating virtual memory as part of RAM.
mistakes.right: Virtual memory is disk space used as overflow. It is slower than RAM.

mistakes.wrong: Picking cache for 'smallest and fastest'.
mistakes.right: Registers are smaller and faster than cache.

subtopics.notes:
### The memory ladder
Fast memory costs more, so a computer has only a little of it. It stacks the types from fast and small to slow and large.

| Level | Technology | Volatile? | Typical size |
|---|---|---|---|
| Registers | Inside the CPU | Yes | Bytes |
| **Cache** (L1, L2, L3) | **SRAM**, on or near the CPU | Yes | KB to MB |
| **Main memory** | **RAM (DRAM)** | Yes | GB |
| SSD | Flash chips | No | 100s of GB |
| Hard disk, tape | Magnetic | No | TB |

Going up the ladder means faster, costlier and smaller.

> **Tip:** Speed order is Registers, Cache, RAM, SSD, HDD, Tape. Size order is the exact reverse.

### Volatile and non-volatile
Volatile memory loses its data when the power goes off. Registers, cache and RAM are volatile.

Non-volatile memory keeps data without power. ROM, flash (SSD, pen drive, memory card), hard disk and DVD are non-volatile.

> **Rule:** ROM is never volatile. Both SRAM and DRAM are volatile.

### RAM, the working desk
RAM holds the programs and data in use right now. You can read and write it freely. Power-off wipes it.

| Type | Full form | Main facts |
|---|---|---|
| **SRAM** | Static RAM | Flip-flop cells. No refresh needed. Fast and costly. Used for **cache**. |
| **DRAM** | Dynamic RAM | One transistor and one capacitor per bit. Cheaper and denser. Used for **main memory**. |

A DRAM capacitor leaks its charge. So DRAM needs constant refreshing. SRAM does not.

### The ROM family
ROM means Read Only Memory. It is non-volatile, and ordinary programs can only read it. The family differs in how each chip is written and erased.

| Type | Written | Erased |
|---|---|---|
| PROM | Once | Never |
| **EPROM** | Reprogrammable | **Ultraviolet (UV) light** |
| **EEPROM** | Reprogrammable | **Electrically**, in the circuit |
| Flash | Reprogrammable in blocks | Electrically (fast) |

SSDs and pen drives are flash. The start-up firmware of a PC (BIOS or UEFI) sits in ROM or flash. That is why it survives every power cut.

> **Tip:** More E's mean more electricity. EPROM is erased by UV light. EEPROM is erased electrically.

### Cache and virtual memory
**Cache** is a small SRAM buffer between the CPU and RAM. It keeps copies of recently used data. So the CPU rarely waits for slow RAM. L1 is smallest and fastest. Then comes L2, then L3.

**Virtual memory** uses disk space as extra RAM when RAM is full. It is called the page file. It stops the machine from crashing. But it is far slower than real RAM.

> **Watch:** Virtual memory is not physical memory. It lives on the storage disk, not inside RAM.

patterns.name: Volatile vs non-volatile identification
patterns.howToSpot: The words 'volatile', 'non-volatile', 'loses data when power is off' or 'permanent'.
steps: Sort each option into volatile or non-volatile.
Volatile: registers, cache, RAM (SRAM and DRAM).
Non-volatile: ROM family, flash, magnetic disk, DVD.
In statement questions, test each memory against this split.
patterns.why: Only memory that needs power to hold its data is volatile.

example.q: Which of the following is non-volatile?
steps: RAM, cache and registers all lose data at power-off.
ROM keeps its content without power.

patterns.name: Hierarchy ordering and cache position
patterns.howToSpot: 'Arrange in order of speed', 'fastest', 'smallest' or 'between CPU and RAM'.
steps: Write the order: Registers, Cache, RAM, SSD, HDD, Tape.
Speed falls as you move right. Size grows.
Cache is the SRAM buffer between CPU and RAM.
'Smallest but fastest' means registers, not cache.
patterns.why: Cost limits how much fast memory a machine can have.

example.q: Arrange by access speed, fastest first: RAM, Registers, Hard disk, Cache.
steps: Registers are inside the CPU, so they are fastest.
Cache comes next, then RAM, then the hard disk.

patterns.name: SRAM vs DRAM
patterns.howToSpot: 'Refresh', 'flip-flop', 'capacitor', 'static', 'dynamic' or 'used for cache'.
steps: DRAM stores each bit in a capacitor that leaks, so it needs refreshing.
DRAM is cheaper and denser. It is main memory.
SRAM uses flip-flops. It is faster and costlier. It is cache.
S is Static (stands still). D is Dynamic (must be refreshed).
patterns.why: The leaking capacitor is the reason DRAM needs refresh.

example.q: DRAM needs to be refreshed periodically because...
steps: Each DRAM bit sits in a tiny capacitor.
The capacitor slowly loses its charge.
So the cells are re-read and re-written again and again.

patterns.name: ROM family: PROM, EPROM, EEPROM, firmware
patterns.howToSpot: 'Programmed only once', 'ultraviolet', 'electrically erasable', 'BIOS' or 'firmware'.
steps: Match the erase method: PROM never, EPROM UV light, EEPROM electrically.
Flash is electrically erased, in blocks.
'Programmed only once' means PROM.
BIOS or firmware lives in ROM or flash, because it must survive power cuts.
patterns.why: Each ROM type is defined by how it is erased.

example.q: Which memory holds the BIOS firmware of a PC?
steps: Firmware must survive every power cut.
So it cannot sit in volatile RAM.

patterns.name: Cache and virtual memory concepts
patterns.howToSpot: 'Page file', 'overflow of RAM', 'L1, L2, L3' or 'copies of frequently used data'.
steps: Cache is a small SRAM buffer between CPU and RAM.
L1 is inside the core: fastest and smallest.
Virtual memory is disk space used as RAM overflow.
It is big but slow. It is not physical RAM.
patterns.why: Cache saves the CPU from waiting. Virtual memory saves the system from running out of RAM.

example.q: Virtual memory is best described as...
steps: When RAM fills up, the OS uses disk space as an overflow area.
That area is the page file.
example.answer: Disk space used as an extension of RAM

patterns.name: Fastest, costliest or largest memory
patterns.howToSpot: 'Fastest memory', 'most expensive per byte' or 'largest capacity'.
steps: Put the memories in ladder order.
Fastest and costliest per byte is at the top: registers.
Largest and cheapest per byte is at the bottom: tape and hard disk.
Read the stem's word: fastest, smallest or largest.
patterns.why: Speed and cost rise together. Size falls.

example.q: Which memory in a computer is the fastest?
steps: Registers are inside the CPU.
They are the top rung of the ladder.

revision: Speed order: Registers, Cache (SRAM), RAM (DRAM), SSD, HDD, Tape.
Volatile: registers, cache, RAM. Non-volatile: ROM, flash, disk.
SRAM is for cache (fast, no refresh). DRAM is for main memory (cheap, needs refresh).
PROM once, EPROM UV erase, EEPROM electrical erase, flash in blocks.
BIOS or UEFI firmware sits in ROM or flash.
Virtual memory is disk acting as RAM overflow, not real RAM.

subtopics.title: Memory units and conversions
subtopics.concept: Data is stored as bits. Eight bits make one byte. Each unit above the byte is 1024 times the one below it. File sizes use bytes (MB, GB). Internet speeds use bits (Mbps). Exams always test this difference.

formulas.name: bits vs bytes
formulas.note: capital B = byte, small b = bit (speeds are usually bits)

tricks.title: The 1024 ladder
tricks.body: Every step up multiplies by 1024 ($2^{10}$), never 1000. Half a KB is 512 B.

example.q: 2 GB = ? KB

tricks.title: Bit or byte speed check
tricks.body: Line speeds are in bits (Mbps). File sizes are in bytes (MB). To get MB per second, divide Mbps by 8.

example.q: A 16 Mbps line moves how many MB per second?
steps: Divide the bits by 8.

mistakes.wrong: Using 1000 instead of 1024 in a ladder question.
mistakes.right: Exams use 1024 at every step.

mistakes.wrong: Reading Mbps as megabytes per second.
mistakes.right: Mbps is megabits. Divide by 8 to get MB per second.

mistakes.wrong: Multiplying by 1024 when going up the ladder.
mistakes.right: Going up (KB to MB) divides by 1024. Going down multiplies.

mistakes.wrong: Forgetting to multiply by 8 when a question asks for bits.
mistakes.right: Bytes to bits is always × 8.

mistakes.wrong: Comparing options in different units.
mistakes.right: Convert all options to one unit before comparing.

subtopics.notes:
### The unit ladder
The smallest unit is the **bit**. It is one 0 or one 1. Above the byte, every step multiplies by **1024**, which is $2^{10}$.

| Unit | Equals |
|---|---|
| 1 Nibble | 4 bits |
| 1 Byte (B) | 8 bits |
| 1 KiloByte (KB) | 1024 B |
| 1 MegaByte (MB) | 1024 KB |
| 1 GigaByte (GB) | 1024 MB |
| 1 TeraByte (TB) | 1024 GB |
| 1 PetaByte (PB) | 1024 TB |

> **Rule:** Exams use 1024, never 1000.

Some exact values to remember. 1 MB is $2^{20}$ = 10,48,576 bytes. 1 GB is $2^{30}$ = 1,07,37,41,824 bytes.

### How to convert
Going up the ladder, divide by 1024. Going down, multiply by 1024.

- 4 GB to MB: 4 × 1024 = **4096 MB**.
- 2048 KB to MB: 2048 ÷ 1024 = **2 MB**.
- Bits in 2 KB: 2 × 1024 = 2048 bytes. Then 2048 × 8 = **16,384 bits**.

> **Tip:** For "which is largest", change every option to the same unit first. KB is usually easiest.

### Bits and bytes in speed questions
File sizes and storage are measured in **bytes** (MB, GB). Line speeds are measured in **bits**. Mbps means megabits per second.

Eight bits make one byte. So an 8 Mbps line moves about 1 MB of file data each second.

> **Watch:** Capital B is a byte. Small b is a bit. Mb is a megabit. MB is a megabyte.

Try a quick one. A plan says 24 Mbps. Divide by 8. You get 3 MB per second. A 30 MB file then needs 10 seconds. Always divide the size in MB by the speed in MB per second.

### Download time in three steps
Take a 10 MB file on a 16 Mbps line.

1. Change the file to bits. 10 × 8 = 80 megabits.
2. Divide by the speed. 80 ÷ 16 = 5.
3. The answer is **5 seconds**.

You can also change the speed to bytes. 16 ÷ 8 = 2 MB per second. Then 10 ÷ 2 = 5 seconds.

### Which option is largest
Take the options 1024 KB, 1 MB, 10,00,000 bytes and 0.5 GB. Put everything in KB.

| Option | In KB |
|---|---|
| 1024 KB | 1024 |
| 1 MB | 1024 |
| 10,00,000 bytes | about 977 |
| 0.5 GB | 5,24,288 |

So **0.5 GB** is the largest.

### Other units you may meet
- **Word length** is the number of bits a CPU handles in one go. A 64-bit processor has a 64-bit word.
- The smallest unit of data is the bit.
- The smallest unit of memory usually addressed is 1 byte.
- Half a byte is a nibble (4 bits). One hexadecimal digit is exactly one nibble.

### Everyday sizes
Use these to reject silly options fast.

- A phone photo is about 2 to 5 MB.
- A movie is about 1 to 4 GB.
- A good laptop SSD is about 512 GB to 1 TB.
- Internet plans are sold in Mbps. Your browser shows MB per second. An 80 Mbps line downloads near 10 MB per second.

patterns.name: Bit, nibble and byte definitions
patterns.howToSpot: 'How many bits in...', 'nibble' or 'smallest unit'.
steps: Remember: 1 byte = 8 bits and 1 nibble = 4 bits.
So one byte is two nibbles.
For bigger counts, multiply. Bits = bytes × 8.
One hex digit equals one nibble.
patterns.why: Every larger unit is built from the byte.

example.q: How many bits are there in 3 bytes?
steps: Each byte has 8 bits.

patterns.name: KB, MB, GB, TB ladder conversion
patterns.howToSpot: 'How many MB in 4 GB', 'convert KB to MB' or 'which is largest'.
steps: Decide: are you going up or down the ladder?
Down: multiply by 1024. Up: divide by 1024.
Do it one rung at a time.
For 'largest', change all options to one unit.
patterns.why: Every rung of the ladder is the same factor, 1024.

example.q: A pen drive holds 4 GB. How many MB is that (exam convention)?
steps: GB to MB goes down one rung.

patterns.name: Bits vs bytes in data-transfer speed
patterns.howToSpot: 'Mbps', 'download time', 'per second' or 'speed of the line'.
steps: Check the units: Mb or MB?
Change the file to bits (× 8), or the speed to bytes (÷ 8).
Divide file size by speed, in the same unit.
8 Mbps equals 1 MB per second.
patterns.why: Speed is measured in bits but files are measured in bytes.

example.q: A connection delivers 16 Mbps. How many megabytes is that per second?
steps: Eight bits make one byte.
So divide 16 by 8.

patterns.name: Unit odd-one-out and definitions
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which is NOT a unit of data size' or 'word length'.
steps: Size units: bit, nibble, byte, KB, MB, GB, TB, PB.
Mbps is a speed unit, not a size unit.
Word length is the bits a CPU processes in one operation.
Cross out the speed unit.
patterns.why: Odd-one-out questions usually hide a speed unit among size units.

example.q: Which of the following is NOT a unit of data size?  KB, MB, Mbps, GB
steps: KB, MB and GB measure size.
Mbps is megabits per second, a speed.

patterns.name: Download time and bit counts
patterns.howToSpot: 'How long to download', 'how many bits in 2 KB' or 'time for a file'.
steps: Write the file size in one unit.
Change bytes to bits with × 8.
Divide bits by the line speed in bits per second.
Check that the units cancel.
patterns.why: Time is size divided by speed, so both must use bits.

example.q: How long will a 10 MB file take on a 16 Mbps line?
steps: 10 MB = 10 × 8 = 80 megabits.

revision: Bit, Nibble (4 bits), Byte (8 bits), KB, MB, GB, TB, PB. Each step is × 1024.
Speeds are in bits. 8 Mbps is about 1 MB per second of file data.
Nibble = 4 bits = one hex digit. Smallest unit is the bit.
Word length is the bits a CPU handles at once.

subtopics.title: Number systems: binary, octal, decimal, hexadecimal
subtopics.concept: A number system is a way of writing numbers with a fixed set of digits. Computers use binary (base 2). People use decimal (base 10). Octal (base 8) and hexadecimal (base 16) are short ways to write binary. Every conversion in the exam follows one of three moves: multiply and add, divide and read upward, or group bits.

formulas.name: Positional value
formulas.note: digit d_i at position i (from 0, rightmost), base b

formulas.name: Decimal to base b
formulas.tex: N = (\ldots r_2 r_1 r_0)_b\ \text{from repeated division by } b

formulas.name: Grouping shortcuts
formulas.note: group binary from the RIGHT; pad with leading zeros

tricks.title: 3 and 4 grouping
tricks.body: Octal uses 3-bit groups. Hex uses 4-bit groups. Both start from the right. Pad the left with zeros. No division is needed.

example.q: Write 11010111 in octal.
steps: Group from the right: 011 010 111.
Read each group: 3, 2, 7.

example.q: Find the decimal value of C8 in hex.
steps: C is 12.

tricks.title: Power-of-2 positions
tricks.body: Memorise 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. Then binary to decimal means adding the places that hold a 1.

example.q: Convert 111010 to decimal.
steps: The 1s are at 32, 16, 8 and 2.

mistakes.wrong: Reading the remainders from top to bottom.
mistakes.right: Read the remainders from bottom to top.

mistakes.wrong: Counting positions from 1 instead of 0.
mistakes.right: The rightmost digit is position 0. Its value is digit × 1.

mistakes.wrong: Grouping bits from the left.
mistakes.right: Group from the right and pad the left with zeros.

mistakes.wrong: Using 3-bit groups for hex or 4-bit groups for octal.
mistakes.right: Octal is 3 bits per digit. Hex is 4 bits per digit.

mistakes.wrong: Treating F as 16.
mistakes.right: F is 15. That is why FF is 255.

mistakes.wrong: Accepting 8 or 9 in an octal number.
mistakes.right: Octal digits stop at 7. Such an option is wrong.

subtopics.notes:
### The four systems
The base is the number of different digits the system uses.

| System | Base | Digits | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Binary | 2 | 0, 1 | 1101 |
| Octal | 8 | 0 to 7 | 65 |
| Decimal | 10 | 0 to 9 | 91 |
| Hexadecimal | 16 | 0 to 9, A to F | 2F |

In hexadecimal, A is 10, B is 11, C is 12, D is 13, E is 14 and F is 15.

### Any base to decimal
Each digit is worth digit × base^position. Count positions from 0 at the right.

$$(1101)_2 = 1\times8 + 1\times4 + 0\times2 + 1\times1 = 13$$

- $(2F)_{16} = 2\times16 + 15 = 47$.
- $(67)_8 = 6\times8 + 7 = 55$.

> **Tip:** Learn the powers of 2: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1024. Then binary to decimal is just adding the places that hold a 1.

### Decimal to any base
Divide again and again by the new base. Write each remainder. Read the remainders from **bottom to top**.

For 45 in binary:

1. 45 ÷ 2 = 22, remainder **1**.
2. 22 ÷ 2 = 11, remainder **0**.
3. 11 ÷ 2 = 5, remainder **1**.
4. 5 ÷ 2 = 2, remainder **1**.
5. 2 ÷ 2 = 1, remainder **0**.
6. 1 ÷ 2 = 0, remainder **1**.

Reading upward gives $(101101)_2$. Check: 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 45.

### Grouping shortcut for octal and hex
One octal digit is 3 bits. One hex digit is 4 bits. Make groups **from the right**. Pad the left with zeros.

- $(1101011)_2$ becomes 001 101 011, which is 1, 5, 3. So it is $(153)_8$.
- $(11011011)_2$ becomes 1101 1011, which is D, B. So it is $(DB)_{16}$.

> **Rule:** Octal uses 3-bit groups. Hex uses 4-bit groups. Always start from the right.

### Ranges and valid digits
n bits hold $2^n$ different values, from 0 to $2^n - 1$. So 8 bits hold 256 values, from 0 to 255.

- FF in hex is 255. It is the largest 8-bit value.
- 777 in octal is 511. It is the largest 3-digit octal number.
- An octal number never has 8 or 9.
- A hex number never has a letter after F.

### More worked pairs
Use these as anchors to test your answers.

- $(1010)_2 = 8 + 2 = 10$.
- $(1111)_2 = 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15$.
- $(255)_{10} = 15\times16 + 15 = (FF)_{16}$.
- $(128)_{10} = (10000000)_2$.
- $(100)_8 = 64$, $(20)_{16} = 32$, $(11)_2 = 3$.
- $(10000)_2 = 16$, because only the 16 place holds a 1.
- $(777)_8 = 7\times64 + 7\times8 + 7 = 511$.

### Quick checks on the options
Strike out options before you calculate.

1. An option with 8 or 9 is never octal.
2. An option with G or beyond is never hexadecimal.
3. A binary number ending in 0 is even. One ending in 1 is odd.

> **Watch:** Check the source base first. A digit that does not exist in that base means the option is wrong.

patterns.name: Any base to decimal
patterns.howToSpot: 'Decimal value of', 'equivalent decimal' or a number written with a subscript base.
steps: Write the position of each digit, from 0 at the right.
Multiply each digit by base^position.
For hex, change letters to numbers first (A = 10 to F = 15).
Add the products.
patterns.why: Each place is worth a power of the base.

example.q: The decimal value of the binary number 110101 is...
steps: The 1s sit at 32, 16, 4 and 1.

patterns.name: Decimal to any base
patterns.howToSpot: 'Binary equivalent of', 'convert decimal to octal' or 'to hex'.
steps: Divide the number by the target base.
Write the remainder. Divide the quotient again.
Stop when the quotient is 0.
Read the remainders bottom to top.
patterns.why: Each remainder is one digit of the new number, starting from the right.

example.q: The binary equivalent of decimal 45 is...
steps: The remainders in order are 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1.
Read them upward: 101101.

patterns.name: Binary to octal or hex by grouping
patterns.howToSpot: 'Binary number in octal' or 'in hexadecimal'.
steps: Octal: group bits in 3s from the right. Hex: group in 4s.
Pad the left with zeros.
Convert each group to one digit.
For hex, write 10 to 15 as A to F.
patterns.why: One octal digit is exactly 3 bits. One hex digit is exactly 4 bits.

example.q: The binary number 1101011 in octal is...
steps: Group in 3s from the right: 001 101 011.
The groups are 1, 5 and 3.

patterns.name: n-bit range and digit validity
patterns.howToSpot: 'How many values can n bits represent', 'largest number' or 'which is a valid octal number'.
steps: n bits give $2^n$ different values.
They run from 0 to $2^n - 1$.
Octal digits are 0 to 7 only.
Hex digits are 0 to 9 and A to F only.
patterns.why: Each extra bit doubles the number of values.

example.q: How many different values can be represented by 8 bits?
steps: Each bit has 2 choices, so the count is $2^8$.
The largest value is one less: 255.

patterns.name: Hex and binary conversions
patterns.howToSpot: A number with letters A to F, or 'hexadecimal equivalent'.
steps: Turn each hex digit into a number (A = 10 to F = 15).
For hex to decimal, use digit × 16^position.
For binary to hex, group in 4s from the right.
Change each group back to a hex digit.
patterns.why: Hex is a short way to write binary, four bits at a time.

example.q: The binary number 11011011 in hexadecimal is...
steps: Group in 4s: 1101 and 1011.
1101 is 13, which is D. 1011 is 11, which is B.

patterns.name: Largest values and anchors
patterns.howToSpot: 'Largest 3-digit octal', 'FF in decimal' or 'value of 10000'.
steps: Use the top digit in every place (7 for octal, F for hex).
Multiply out by the place values.
Or use the anchors: FF is 255, 777 in octal is 511.
Check by adding 1 to reach the next power.
patterns.why: Every base has one largest number for each number of digits.

example.q: What is the decimal value of the octal number 777?

revision: Bases: binary 2 (0, 1), octal 8 (0 to 7), decimal 10, hex 16 (0 to 9, A to F).
To decimal: digit × base^position, positions from 0 at the right.
From decimal: divide by the base, read remainders bottom to top.
Octal is 3-bit groups. Hex is 4-bit groups. Group from the right.
F = 15. FF = 255. 8 bits give 256 values (0 to 255).
Octal has no 8 or 9. Hex has nothing after F.

subtopics.title: Input and output devices
subtopics.concept: An input device sends data or commands into the computer. An output device brings results out. Some devices, such as a touch screen, do both. Exams ask you to sort devices, match each device to its job, and tell impact printers from non-impact printers.

tricks.title: Marks, Characters, Ink
tricks.body: OMR is Marks (bubbles). OCR is Characters (text). MICR is Ink on cheques (banks). Match the noun in the question.

example.q: Which reader is used for bank cheques?
steps: Cheques carry magnetic ink characters.
That is MICR.

tricks.title: Impact means hit
tricks.body: If a printer physically hits the paper (dot matrix, daisy wheel), it is impact. It is noisy but can make copies. Inkjet, laser and thermal never strike the paper.

example.q: Which is a non-impact printer: dot matrix or laser?
steps: Dot matrix pins strike the ribbon.
A laser fuses toner without hitting.

mistakes.wrong: Calling a scanner or microphone an output device.
mistakes.right: Scanner, camera and microphone send data in. They are input devices.

mistakes.wrong: Choosing 'touch screen' as output only.
mistakes.right: A touch screen is both input and output.

mistakes.wrong: Mixing up OMR, OCR and MICR.
mistakes.right: OMR is marks, OCR is characters, MICR is magnetic ink on cheques.

mistakes.wrong: Calling a laser printer an impact printer.
mistakes.right: Laser, inkjet and thermal printers are non-impact.

mistakes.wrong: Calling a monitor's display a hard copy.
mistakes.right: Monitor output is soft copy. Paper output is hard copy.

subtopics.notes:
### Input devices
An input device feeds data or commands **into** the computer.

| Group | Devices |
|---|---|
| Typing and pointing | Keyboard, mouse, trackball, touchpad, joystick, light pen, stylus |
| Capture | Scanner, digital camera, webcam, microphone |
| Readers | Barcode or QR reader, OMR, OCR, MICR, biometric scanner |

> **Tip:** OMR reads **marks** (pencil bubbles). OCR reads **characters** (printed text). MICR reads **magnetic ink** on cheques.

### Output devices
An output device brings results **out** of the computer.

| Device | What it gives |
|---|---|
| **Monitor** | **Soft copy**: you can see it but not touch it |
| **Printer** | **Hard copy**: output on paper |
| Speaker, headphones | Sound |
| **Plotter** | Hard copy of large drawings and maps |
| Projector | A big soft copy on a screen |

A 3D printer builds a solid object layer by layer. It is also an output device.

### Impact and non-impact printers
An impact printer physically strikes the paper through a ribbon. A non-impact printer does not hit the paper.

| Type | How it works | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Impact** | Strikes the paper | Dot matrix, daisy wheel |
| **Non-impact** | Sprays ink, fuses toner or heats paper | Laser, inkjet, thermal |

Impact printers are noisy and cheap. They can print multi-copy forms. Laser printers use toner and are fast. Inkjet printers use liquid ink.

> **Rule:** If the printer hits the paper, it is impact. Dot matrix is the standard example.

### Devices that do both
A **touch screen** takes your finger as input and shows output. A headset has a microphone (input) and speakers (output).

> **Watch:** Touch screen is the standard answer to "both input and output". It is also the trap inside output-only lists.

### Pointing devices
- **Mouse:** the standard pointing device. A ball or an optical sensor tracks movement.
- **Trackball:** an upside-down mouse. You roll the ball and the device stays still.
- **Touchpad:** the flat mouse replacement on a laptop.
- **Joystick:** direction control for games and flight simulators.
- **Light pen and stylus:** draw or point directly on the screen.

Every pointing device sends position data in. So all of them are input devices.

### Device and use pairs
| Device | Classic use |
|---|---|
| Barcode reader | Supermarket billing |
| OMR | Checking pencil-bubble answer sheets |
| MICR | Reading the code line on bank cheques |
| OCR | Turning a scanned page into editable text |
| Biometric scanner | Attendance, Aadhaar-style identity checks |
| Plotter | Engineering drawings, maps, posters |
| Webcam and microphone | Video calls |

patterns.name: Input device identification
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which is an input device' or a list with one device that sends data in.
steps: Ask: does data flow into the computer or out of it?
Scanner, microphone and camera are input devices.
Monitor, printer, speaker, plotter and projector are output devices.
Pick the option that feeds data in.
patterns.why: The direction of data flow decides the class.

example.q: Which of the following is an input device?  Monitor, Scanner, Plotter, Speaker
steps: Monitor, plotter and speaker all send data out.
A scanner brings a paper document in as an image.

patterns.name: Output devices, soft copy and hard copy
patterns.howToSpot: 'Soft copy', 'hard copy', 'printout' or 'displayed on screen'.
steps: Soft copy is on a screen: monitor, projector.
Hard copy is on paper: printer, plotter.
Speaker and headphones give sound output.
Watch for the touch screen trap.
patterns.why: Hard copy is permanent and touchable. Soft copy is not.

example.q: Output shown on paper is called a...
steps: Paper output can be touched and kept.
That is a hard copy.

patterns.name: Both input and output, odd one out
patterns.howToSpot: 'Both input and output' or 'which is NOT an input device'.
steps: Classify every option as input, output or both.
Both: touch screen, headset.
For 'not an input', look for a printer, monitor or speaker.
Use the table, not guesswork.
patterns.why: A device that takes and gives data is both.

example.q: Which device acts as both an input and an output device?
steps: Your touch is input.
The display is output.

patterns.name: Printer types and reader classification
patterns.howToSpot: 'Impact printer', 'non-impact', 'plotter' or 'OMR, OCR, MICR'.
steps: Impact means a physical strike: dot matrix, daisy wheel.
Non-impact: laser, inkjet, thermal.
Readers: OMR marks, OCR characters, MICR magnetic ink.
Plotter draws large drawings. A 3D printer builds objects.
patterns.why: Each printer type is defined by how it puts marks on paper.

example.q: Which of the following is an impact printer?
steps: Dot matrix pins strike the ribbon against the paper.
Laser, inkjet and thermal never hit the paper.

patterns.name: Device and use matching
patterns.howToSpot: 'Used for', 'used in a supermarket', 'answer sheets' or 'cheque'.
steps: Underline the job in the question.
Find the device with that job in the pairs table.
Barcode is billing. OMR is answer sheets. MICR is cheques.
Biometric is identity. Plotter is large drawings.
patterns.why: Each device has one classic job in exams.

example.q: Which device is used to check pencil-bubble answer sheets?
steps: Pencil bubbles are marks.
The reader for marks is OMR.

revision: Input: keyboard, mouse, scanner, microphone, camera, barcode, OMR, OCR, MICR, biometrics.
OMR is marks. OCR is characters. MICR is magnetic ink (cheques).
Output: monitor (soft copy), printer and plotter (hard copy), speaker, projector.
Impact printers hit the paper (dot matrix). Non-impact are laser, inkjet and thermal.
Touch screen is both input and output. A 3D printer makes solid objects.

subtopics.title: Ports and connectors
subtopics.concept: A port is a socket on the computer where a cable or device plugs in. Each port has one job, such as video, network or keyboard. Exams ask which port fits which job. Learn the job of each port and the serial and parallel difference.

tricks.title: Serial is a single lane
tricks.body: Serial sends one bit at a time over few wires. It suits long distance. Parallel sends a whole byte across 8 wires. It suits short distance, like old printers.

example.q: Which port transmits one bit at a time?
steps: One bit at a time means a single lane.

tricks.title: VGA or HDMI
tricks.body: VGA carries video only and is analog with 15 pins. HDMI is digital and carries audio and video together. 'Sound and picture together' means HDMI.

example.q: Which port carries digital audio and video?
steps: VGA has no audio.
HDMI carries both.

mistakes.wrong: Saying a serial port sends 8 bits at once.
mistakes.right: Serial sends 1 bit at a time. Parallel sends 8 bits.

mistakes.wrong: Choosing VGA for a stem that mentions sound.
mistakes.right: VGA is video only. HDMI or DisplayPort carries audio too.

mistakes.wrong: Thinking VGA is digital.
mistakes.right: VGA is analog. HDMI and DisplayPort are digital.

mistakes.wrong: Saying you must restart to plug in USB.
mistakes.right: USB is hot-swappable. You plug it in while the computer runs.

mistakes.wrong: Confusing the Ethernet port with the audio jack.
mistakes.right: Ethernet (RJ-45) is the wide socket for the network cable. The 3.5 mm jack is for sound.

subtopics.notes:
### What a port is
A **port** is a socket on the cabinet. A cable or device plugs into it. Every port has a job: carry video, join a network, take a keyboard.

Ask one question in the exam: what does the stem want the port to carry?

- Video: VGA, HDMI, DisplayPort.
- Network: Ethernet.
- Old keyboard and mouse: PS/2.
- Everything else today: USB.
- Sound: the 3.5 mm audio jack.

### Serial and parallel ports
| | Serial port | Parallel port |
|---|---|---|
| Bits per transfer | **One bit at a time** | **A whole byte (8 bits) at once** |
| Wires | Few | Many |
| Distance | Long, less interference | Short |
| Classic use | Old modems and mice (COM port) | Old printers (LPT port) |

> **Tip:** Serial is a single lane. Parallel is a multi-lane highway.

### The port table
| Port | Job |
|---|---|
| **USB** (Universal Serial Bus) | Pen drives, keyboards, phones. Hot-swappable. Supplies 5 V power. |
| **HDMI** | Digital video and audio in one cable |
| **VGA** | Analog video only. 15 pins, blue. No sound. |
| **DisplayPort** | Digital video and audio |
| **Ethernet (RJ-45)** | Wired network or LAN |
| **PS/2** | Round 6-pin socket for old keyboard and mouse |
| **Audio jack (3.5 mm)** | Speakers, headphones, microphone |
| **Serial (COM or RS-232)** | One-bit-at-a-time old data link |
| **Parallel (LPT)** | Old 25-pin printer port |

On the audio jack, green is for output and pink is for the microphone.

### USB facts
- **Hot-swappable** means you connect or remove it while the computer runs. No restart is needed.
- USB **supplies power**. So pen drives and small keyboards need no adapter.
- Speeds grow with each version. USB 2.0 is about 480 Mbps. USB 3.0 is about 5 Gbps.
- USB Type-C is the small, reversible oval plug on phones and laptops.

### Stem words and their answers
| Stem words | Answer |
|---|---|
| Picture and sound, one digital cable | HDMI |
| Old blue connector, video only | VGA |
| One bit at a time | Serial (COM) |
| Printer port of old machines | Parallel (LPT) |
| Network cable socket | Ethernet or RJ-45 |
| Round old keyboard and mouse sockets | PS/2 |
| Plug in without restarting | USB |
| Speakers, green round hole | 3.5 mm audio jack |

### A 10-second method
1. Underline the job in the stem: video, sound, network or data direction.
2. Match that job to a row in the port table.
3. If two options look close, drop the one that lacks a feature the stem asks for.

> **Watch:** VGA fails any stem that mentions audio. Parallel fails any stem that mentions long distance.

patterns.name: Serial vs parallel comparison
patterns.howToSpot: 'One bit at a time', 'byte at once', 'COM port' or 'LPT port'.
steps: Serial: 1 bit at a time, few wires, long distance.
Parallel: 8 bits (a byte) at once, short distance.
Parallel was the old printer port (LPT).
In statements, check each number for a reversal.
patterns.why: The two ports differ in how many bits move together.

example.q: A parallel port transfers how much data per transfer?
steps: A parallel port has 8 wires side by side.
So a whole byte moves at once.

patterns.name: Port identification by purpose
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which port connects...' or 'used to connect a...'.
steps: Underline the job in the stem.
Network: Ethernet or RJ-45.
Digital audio and video: HDMI or DisplayPort.
Old keyboard and mouse: PS/2. Speakers: 3.5 mm jack.
patterns.why: Ports are defined by what they carry.

example.q: Which port connects a computer to a wired LAN?
steps: A LAN needs a network cable.
That cable plugs into the RJ-45 socket.

patterns.name: USB facts
patterns.howToSpot: 'Hot-swappable', 'supplies power' or 'USB 3.0 speed'.
steps: Hot-swappable: plug and unplug while the PC runs.
USB carries 5 V power with the data.
USB 2.0 is about 480 Mbps. USB 3.0 is about 5 Gbps.
Type-C is the small reversible plug.
patterns.why: USB is the universal port on modern machines.

example.q: USB is called hot-swappable because...
steps: You can connect or remove a device while the computer runs.
No shutdown or restart is needed.
example.answer: It can be plugged in or removed while the computer is running

patterns.name: Display and audio ports
patterns.howToSpot: 'Analog video only', 'audio and video', 'green socket' or 'pink socket'.
steps: VGA is analog, video only, 15 pins.
HDMI and DisplayPort are digital and carry video and audio.
On the audio jack, green is output for speakers.
Pink is the microphone.
patterns.why: Only HDMI and DisplayPort carry sound with video.

example.q: Which port carries analog video only, with no audio?
steps: It is the 15-pin blue connector.
HDMI and DisplayPort are digital, so they are out.

patterns.name: Old ports: PS/2, COM and LPT
patterns.howToSpot: 'Round 6-pin', 'legacy', 'RS-232' or '25-pin'.
steps: PS/2 is a round 6-pin socket for keyboard and mouse.
COM (RS-232) is the serial port.
LPT is the 25-pin parallel printer port.
Match the shape or pin count to the port.
patterns.why: These ports are old, but exams still ask their names.

example.q: Which port was used for the keyboard and mouse of old PCs?
steps: It is a round 6-pin socket.
That is the PS/2 port.

revision: Serial: 1 bit at a time, long distance (COM). Parallel: 8 bits at once, printers (LPT).
HDMI is digital audio and video. VGA is analog video only.
Ethernet (RJ-45) is for the network. PS/2 is old keyboard and mouse. 3.5 mm is audio.
USB is hot-swappable and supplies power (5 V).
USB 2.0 is about 480 Mbps. USB 3.0 is about 5 Gbps.

subtopics.title: Storage and backup media
subtopics.concept: Primary memory (RAM and cache) is fast but small. Secondary storage is large, permanent and cheaper per GB. Secondary storage comes in three kinds: magnetic, optical and flash. Exams ask capacities, the HDD and SSD difference, and backup methods.

tricks.title: Optical capacity ladder
tricks.body: CD is 700 MB. DVD is 4.7 GB. Blu-ray is 25 GB (single layer). Say it as '700, 4.7, 25'.

example.q: What is the capacity of a single-layer DVD?
steps: The DVD is the middle rung of the ladder.

tricks.title: SSD or HDD in one line
tricks.body: SSD has no moving parts. It is silent, shock-proof, faster and costlier per GB. HDD has spinning platters and gives cheap bulk storage.

example.q: Which storage has no moving parts?
steps: Flash chips have nothing that spins.

mistakes.wrong: Giving 4.7 GB as the capacity of a CD.
mistakes.right: A CD holds 700 MB. 4.7 GB is a DVD.

mistakes.wrong: Calling a hard disk an optical medium.
mistakes.right: A hard disk is magnetic. CD, DVD and Blu-ray are optical.

mistakes.wrong: Saying an SSD has spinning platters.
mistakes.right: An SSD uses flash chips. HDDs have the platters.

mistakes.wrong: Thinking tape gives random access.
mistakes.right: Tape is sequential. Disks and SSDs are random access.

mistakes.wrong: Thinking formatting adds capacity.
mistakes.right: Formatting only prepares the file system.

subtopics.notes:
### Primary and secondary storage
Primary memory (RAM and cache) is fast but small. RAM is also volatile. Secondary storage is large and permanent. It costs less per GB. Everything below is secondary storage.

### The three technologies
| Family | How it stores | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Magnetic** | Magnetised spots on spinning platters or tape | HDD, old floppy, magnetic tape (LTO) |
| **Optical** | Tiny pits read by a **laser** | CD, DVD, Blu-ray |
| **Flash** | Memory chips with no moving parts | SSD, pen drive, memory card, phone storage |

### Optical disc capacities
This row is the exam favourite.

| Disc | Capacity (single layer) | Laser |
|---|---|---|
| **CD** | **700 MB** | Infrared or red |
| **DVD** | **4.7 GB** (dual layer about 8.5 GB) | Red |
| **Blu-ray** | **25 GB** (dual layer about 50 GB) | **Blue-violet** |

The order is CD (0.7 GB), then DVD (4.7 GB), then Blu-ray (25 GB). A blue-violet laser has a shorter wavelength. So it reads tighter pits and stores more data.

> **Tip:** Remember "700, 4.7, 25". A CD holding 4.7 GB should feel wrong at once.

### HDD and SSD
| | HDD | SSD |
|---|---|---|
| Parts | Spinning magnetic platters and moving heads | Flash chips, no moving parts |
| Speed | Slower (heads must seek) | Much faster |
| Shock and noise | Sensitive, some noise | Shock-resistant, silent |
| Cost per GB | Cheaper | Costlier |

> **Rule:** "No moving parts" in a question means SSD.

### Choosing a medium
- Need speed, silence and shock resistance: SSD.
- Need cheap bulk storage: HDD.
- Need to keep archives for years at low cost: magnetic tape.
- Need to carry small files: pen drive or memory card.

### Access methods
- **Random (direct) access:** jump straight to any address. RAM, HDD and SSD work this way.
- **Sequential access:** read in order, like a cassette. Magnetic tape works this way.

Tape is cheap. So it suits archival backups, not daily use.

### Backup ideas
- **Cloud storage or backup:** your files are copied to internet servers. You can reach them from anywhere.
- **Tape libraries:** banks and research labs still archive petabytes on tape.
- **The 3-2-1 habit:** three copies, on two media, with one copy off-site.

### Small facts exams quote
- A **floppy disk** stored 1.44 MB. It is obsolete but still asked.
- A **memory card** is flash storage for cameras and phones (SD, microSD).
- Blu-ray gets its name from the blue-violet laser.
- **Formatting** prepares a disk's file system. It does not add capacity.
- Everyday anchors: an MP3 song is about 4 to 8 MB. A phone holds about 64 to 256 GB.

patterns.name: Optical media capacity matching
patterns.howToSpot: 'Capacity of a CD, DVD or Blu-ray' or 'blue-violet laser'.
steps: Recall the row: CD 700 MB, DVD 4.7 GB, Blu-ray 25 GB.
Dual layer: DVD about 8.5 GB, Blu-ray about 50 GB.
For ordering, use CD, then DVD, then Blu-ray.
Blue-violet laser means Blu-ray.
patterns.why: Shorter laser wavelength packs data tighter.

example.q: A single-layer DVD stores about...
steps: The 700 MB figure is a CD.
25 GB is Blu-ray.

patterns.name: HDD vs SSD vs flash
patterns.howToSpot: 'No moving parts', 'faster', 'spinning platters' or 'shock-resistant'.
steps: HDD: spinning magnetic platters and heads.
SSD and pen drive: flash chips, no moving parts.
SSD is faster, silent and shock-resistant.
Flash keeps data without power.
patterns.why: Moving parts make an HDD slower than an SSD.

example.q: Why is an SSD faster than an HDD?
steps: An SSD has no platters to spin.
It has no heads to seek.

patterns.name: Backup and access methods
patterns.howToSpot: 'Sequential', 'random access', 'archival' or 'cloud backup'.
steps: Archival backup: magnetic tape, cheapest per TB.
Sequential means read in order (tape).
Random means jump to any address (disk, SSD).
Copies on internet servers are cloud backup.
patterns.why: Access method decides how fast a medium finds data.

example.q: Which storage medium uses sequential access?
steps: The drive must wind past earlier data.
Disks and SSDs jump directly instead.

patterns.name: Media odd-one-out and matching
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which is NOT an optical medium' or 'match the medium to its type'.
steps: Optical: CD, DVD, Blu-ray.
Magnetic: HDD, floppy, tape.
Flash: SSD, pen drive, memory card.
Find the option that breaks the family.
patterns.why: Each medium belongs to exactly one family.

example.q: Which of the following is NOT an optical storage medium?  CD, DVD, Hard disk, Blu-ray
steps: CD, DVD and Blu-ray are read by lasers.
A hard disk is magnetic.

patterns.name: Primary vs secondary storage
patterns.howToSpot: 'Secondary storage', 'permanent', 'primary memory' or 'formatting'.
steps: Primary memory: RAM and cache. Fast and small.
Secondary storage: disks, tape, flash. Large and permanent.
Formatting prepares the file system only.
Use everyday sizes to reject silly options.
patterns.why: Primary is for speed. Secondary is for keeping data.

example.q: Which of these is secondary storage?  RAM, Cache, SSD, Registers
steps: RAM, cache and registers are primary memory.
An SSD keeps data without power.

revision: Magnetic: HDD, tape. Optical: CD, DVD, Blu-ray. Flash: SSD, pen drive, memory card.
CD 700 MB, DVD 4.7 GB (dual 8.5 GB), Blu-ray 25 GB (dual 50 GB).
Blu-ray uses a blue-violet laser.
SSD has no moving parts and is faster and costlier. HDD is cheaper per GB.
Tape is sequential and used for archival backup. Disk and SSD are random access.
Cloud backup keeps copies on internet servers. A floppy held 1.44 MB.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: '4 GB = how many MB?', 'bits in a byte/nibble', 'which is largest: 1024 KB / 1 MB / …', or a speed question mixing megabits with megabytes.
pyqPatterns.approach: Convert step by step with the ×1024 ladder (bit → byte → KB → MB → GB → TB), never 1000. For speed questions, remember line speeds are in bits: divide Mbps by 8 to get megabytes per second. For 'which is largest', convert every option to one unit first.

example.q: How many MB are there in 2 GB?
example.solution: 2 × 1024 = 2048 MB — each step up the ladder multiplies by 1024.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'The decimal value of (1101)₂', 'the binary equivalent of 45', '(11011011)₂ in hexadecimal', 'how many values can 8 bits represent'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Base→decimal: digit × base^position from the right. Decimal→base: divide repeatedly and read remainders bottom-to-top. Binary→octal/hex: group in 3s or 4s from the right. Always verify by converting back. Digit validity is a free elimination: no 8/9 in octal, nothing after F in hex.

example.q: The binary equivalent of decimal 45 is:
example.solution: Divide by 2 and read remainders upward: 101101. Check: 32+8+4+1 = 45.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Which is volatile?', 'EPROM is erased by…', 'where is the BIOS stored?', 'SRAM vs DRAM refresh', 'cache lies where?'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Volatile = vanishes with power (registers, cache, RAM). Non-volatile = ROM family, flash, disk. ROM ladder: PROM once → EPROM (UV) → EEPROM (electrically) → flash. SRAM = cache (no refresh); DRAM = main memory (needs refresh); virtual memory = disk overflow, not RAM.

example.q: EPROM differs from PROM because it can be erased by:
example.solution: Ultraviolet light — EEPROM goes one step further and erases electrically.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Which port carries audio + video?', 'one bit at a time', 'RJ-45 is for…', 'hot-swappable means…', 'which port for the old keyboard?'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Port table recall: HDMI = digital video + audio, VGA = analog video only, Ethernet/RJ-45 = network, PS/2 = old keyboard/mouse, USB = universal + hot-swap + power. Serial = 1 bit at a time over long runs; parallel = 8 bits, the old printer (LPT) port.

example.q: Which port connects a computer to a wired LAN?
example.solution: The Ethernet port (RJ-45) — the tabbed socket for the network cable.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Which is an impact printer?', 'OMR/OCR/MICR reads what?', 'plotter is used for', '3D printer produces'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Impact = physically strikes (dot matrix, daisy wheel); non-impact = laser, inkjet, thermal. Readers by one word: OMR marks, OCR characters, MICR magnetic ink on cheques. Plotter = large drawings; 3D printer = solid objects layer by layer.

example.q: Which is an impact printer?
example.solution: Dot matrix — its pins strike the ribbon against the paper; laser and inkjet never hit.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Which is an input device?', 'which is NOT an input device?', 'soft copy vs hard copy', 'which device is both input and output?'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Direction test: data flowing INTO the computer = input (keyboard, mouse, scanner, mic, readers, biometrics); results OUT = output (monitor, printer, speaker, plotter, projector). Soft copy = screen; hard copy = paper. Touch screen does both — the standard both-direction answer.

example.q: A printout on paper is called a:
example.solution: Hard copy — permanent output; a monitor's display is a soft copy.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Capacity of a CD/DVD/Blu-ray', 'which storage has no moving parts', 'sequential access example', 'match medium to technology'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Capacity row: CD 700 MB, DVD 4.7 GB (dual 8.5), Blu-ray 25 GB with its blue-violet laser. Technology families: magnetic (HDD, tape), optical (CD/DVD/BD), flash (SSD, pen drive, card). Tape = sequential access, archival; disk/SSD = random access; SSD beats HDD on speed, loses on cost per GB.

example.q: A single-layer Blu-ray disc stores about:
example.solution: 25 GB — its short-wavelength blue-violet laser packs far more data than a DVD's red laser.

solvedExamples.q: What is the decimal equivalent of the binary number 1011011?
solvedExamples.solution: Write positional powers of 2 under the digits: 1x64 + 0x32 + 1x16 + 1x8 + 0x4 + 1x2 + 1x1 = 64+16+8+2+1 = 91.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Powers row 64 32 16 8 4 2 1; pick the positions with 1s: 64+16+8+2+1 = 91. (Verified computationally.)

solvedExamples.q: The decimal number 58 in binary is:
solvedExamples.solution: Repeated division by 2: 58->29 r0, 29->14 r1, 14->7 r0, 7->3 r1, 3->1 r1, 1->0 r1. Reading remainders bottom to top: 111010. Check: 32+16+8+2 = 58.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Subtract powers of 2 from 58: 32 leaves 26, 16 leaves 10, 8 leaves 2, 2 leaves 0 -> bits at 32,16,8,2 -> 111010.

solvedExamples.q: The octal equivalent of the binary number 11010111 is:
solvedExamples.solution: Group the bits in threes from the right: 011 010 111. Convert each group: 011=3, 010=2, 111=7, giving 327 (octal). Cross-check: 327 in octal = 3x64+2x8+7 = 215 = value of 11010111 in decimal.
solvedExamples.shortcut: 3-bit groups from the right; pad the left with zero. Octal digits can never include 8 or 9 - that kills two options instantly.

solvedExamples.q: How many megabytes are there in 4 GB (exam convention)?
solvedExamples.solution: 1 GB = 1024 MB, so 4 GB = 4 x 1024 = 4096 MB. In powers of two: 4 GB = 2^2 x 2^30 B = 2^32 B = 2^22 KB x 1024 = 4096 MB.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Each ladder step is x1024, so GB->MB is just 4 x 1024 = 4096. Options 1024/2048/8192 are the x1024 answers for 1, 2 and 8 GB - read the question's number carefully.

solvedExamples.q: Which of the following devices reads the characters printed at the bottom of bank cheques using magnetic ink?
solvedExamples.solution: MICR (Magnetic Ink Character Recognition) reads the 9-digit code printed in iron-oxide ink along a cheque's bottom strip. OCR reads ordinary printed text, OMR reads pencil marks/bubbles, barcode readers read retail bar patterns.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Cheque -> MICR (Ink). Marks -> OMR. Characters -> OCR. Bars -> barcode.

practice.q: A nibble consists of how many bits?
practice.solution: A nibble is half a byte: 4 bits. A byte is 8 bits; a word is CPU-dependent (16/32/64 bits).
practice.shortcut: Nibble = half a byte = 4 bits ('nybble nibbles off half').

practice.q: Which of the following is a volatile memory?
practice.solution: DRAM (dynamic RAM) loses its contents the moment power is cut. The ROM family (PROM, EPROM, EEPROM) and flash-based SSDs are non-volatile.
practice.shortcut: Volatile = Vanishes: registers, cache, RAM. Everything with 'ROM' or flash in the name stays put.

practice.q: The small, very fast memory placed between the CPU and main memory is:
practice.solution: Cache (usually SRAM, levels L1-L3) stores frequently used data between the CPU and RAM. Virtual memory is disk-based overflow; buffers smooth I/O transfers; CMOS holds BIOS settings.
practice.shortcut: 'Between CPU and RAM' is the exact address of cache.

practice.q: EPROM differs from PROM because it can be erased by:
practice.solution: EPROM (Erasable Programmable ROM) is erased by exposing the quartz window to ultraviolet light. PROM cannot be erased once programmed; EEPROM is the electrically erasable version.
practice.shortcut: One E = light (EPROM, UV); two E's = electricity (EEPROM).

practice.q: The decimal value of the binary number 111010 is:
The binary equivalent of decimal 156 is:
The decimal number 200 in hexadecimal is:
practice.shortcut: Divide by 16: 200/16 = 12 r 8 -> C8. The remainder is the last hex digit, the quotient the first.

practice.q: The hexadecimal number 2F equals which decimal number?
practice.shortcut: F=15: so 32+15 = 47. Options built from F=5, 7 or 13 are the traps.

practice.q: The largest decimal number that can be stored in 8 binary bits is:
practice.solution: 11111111 = 2^8 - 1 = 255. (256 needs 9 bits; 127 is the largest for 7-bit or the max of a signed 8-bit byte.)
practice.shortcut: n bits -> largest unsigned value 2^n - 1. 8 bits -> 255.

practice.q: Which input device is used to evaluate answers marked with pencil bubbles on an OMR answer sheet?
practice.solution: OMR (Optical Mark Recognition) detects the presence/absence of marks in fixed positions - exactly the bubble-sheet use case.
practice.shortcut: Bubbles/marks -> OMR. Printed text -> OCR. Cheques -> MICR. Plotter is an output device.

practice.q: Which of the following is a non-impact printer?
practice.solution: Laser printers form images with electrostatic toner - no physical strike - so they are non-impact (as are inkjet and thermal). Dot matrix and daisy wheel strike an inked ribbon.
practice.shortcut: Impact family is short: dot matrix + daisy wheel. Almost every other printer is non-impact.

practice.q: A hard copy of large engineering drawings is best produced on a:
practice.solution: Plotters draw precise, large-format line art (A0/A1 sheets) with a pen or cutting head - standard for CAD output. Printers handle page-size documents; a scanner is an input device.

practice.q: Which port carries digital audio and video signals over a single cable to a monitor or TV?
practice.solution: HDMI transmits uncompressed digital video plus audio in one cable. VGA is analog video-only, PS/2 is for keyboard/mouse, and serial COM ports carry slow bit-serial data.
practice.shortcut: Audio AND video together -> HDMI (or DisplayPort, if listed).

practice.q: The port that transmits data one bit at a time as a single stream, traditionally used for slow data over long distances, is the:
practice.solution: A serial port (COM/RS-232) sends bits sequentially over one channel - slower but reliable over longer cable runs. Parallel ports send a byte across 8 wires simultaneously but only over short distances.
practice.shortcut: 'One bit at a time / single stream' = serial, word for word.

practice.q: Which statement about SSDs and HDDs is correct?
options: SSDs use flash memory with no moving parts
HDDs are always faster than SSDs
practice.solution: An SSD stores data in NAND flash chips with no mechanical parts, making it faster and shock-resistant; an HDD stores data magnetically on spinning platters with a moving head, and is slower but cheaper per GB.
practice.shortcut: 'No moving parts' -> SSD, always. Any option giving moving parts to SSD or calling HDD faster is upside down.

practice.q: Which of the following is **volatile** memory?
practice.solution: **RAM** loses all its content the moment power is cut — the definition of volatile. ROM, flash and DVD are non-volatile.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. Cache memory is volatile.
2. ROM is used to store start-up firmware.
3. The content of RAM survives a system shutdown.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Cache (SRAM) is volatile and ROM holds the BIOS firmware — both correct. Statement 3 is wrong: RAM is volatile, so shutdown wipes it.
practice.shortcut: One vanishing statement ruins the set — RAM never survives.

practice.q: Which shows memories in **decreasing order of speed**?
practice.solution: Speed falls as you move away from the CPU: **Registers → Cache → RAM → Hard disk** (size and cheapness rise in the same direction).

practice.q: **L1, L2 and L3** are levels of —
practice.solution: L1/L2/L3 are the levels of **cache** — small SRAM buffers between the CPU and RAM. L1 is smallest and fastest; L3 is the largest and slowest of the three.

practice.q: Arrange in **increasing** order of access time: A. DRAM  B. SRAM cache  C. Registers  D. Hard disk
practice.solution: Slowest first: hard disk (D), then DRAM (A), then SRAM cache (B), and registers (C) are fastest. Increasing access time = slow → fast = **D, A, B, C**.
practice.shortcut: Disk, DRAM, SRAM, registers — away from the CPU is slow.

practice.q: **SRAM** is preferred for cache memory mainly because it —
options: Is faster and needs no refreshing
practice.solution: SRAM's flip-flop cells answer instantly and **stay valid without refresh** — perfect for cache — but cost more and hold fewer bits per chip than DRAM.
practice.shortcut: S = Static = stands still, no refresh.

practice.q: The full form of **DRAM** hints at its weakness. DRAM stands for —
practice.solution: **DRAM = Dynamic Random Access Memory** — 'dynamic' because its capacitor cells must be **dynamically refreshed** thousands of times per second.

practice.q: Which ROM can be **erased electrically**, without ultraviolet light?
practice.solution: **EEPROM = Electrically Erasable Programmable ROM** — erased by applying an electrical signal in the circuit. EPROM needs a UV lamp; PROM cannot be erased at all.

practice.q: Which statement about **PROM** is correct?
options: It can be erased with UV light
It is faster than all RAM
It can be written (programmed) only once
practice.solution: **PROM** (Programmable ROM) is programmed exactly once after manufacture; after that it is permanent. UV erasing is EPROM's feature; volatility belongs to RAM.

practice.q: The small, very fast memory placed **between the CPU and main memory** is —
practice.solution: **Cache** (SRAM) holds copies of the most-used data so the CPU rarely waits for slower RAM.

practice.q: Cache memory is normally built using —
practice.solution: Cache uses **SRAM** for its speed and zero-refresh cells. DRAM (cheaper, denser) fills main memory instead.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. Virtual memory is a part of physical RAM.
2. Cache memory lies between the CPU and main memory.
3. L1 cache is smaller and faster than L3 cache.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Statements 2 and 3 are standard cache facts. Statement 1 is the classic error — virtual memory is **disk space** used as a RAM overflow, not physical RAM.
practice.shortcut: Virtual = on disk; cache = near CPU.

practice.q: One **byte** consists of how many bits?
practice.solution: **1 byte = 8 bits** — the definition every other conversion builds on.

practice.q: How many **nibbles** make one byte?
practice.solution: A nibble is 4 bits, a byte is 8 bits — so one byte = **2 nibbles**.

practice.q: A short message of **3 bytes** contains how many **bits**?
practice.solution: 3 bytes × 8 bits = **24 bits**. Multiply by 8 to go from bytes to bits.

practice.q: How many **megabytes** are there in **2 GB**?
practice.solution: 2 × 1024 = **2048 MB** — each step up the ladder multiplies by 1024, never 1000.

practice.q: A movie file of **4 GB** equals how many **MB**?
practice.solution: 4 GB = 4 × 1024 = **4096 MB**. The 4000 option is the classic 1000-based trap.

practice.q: **2048 KB** equals —
practice.solution: 2048 ÷ 1024 = **2 MB**. Going up the ladder means dividing by 1024.

practice.q: One **gigabyte** equals how many **megabytes**?
A folder contains **3 files of 512 KB each**. The total size is —
practice.solution: 3 × 512 = 1536 KB; 1536 ÷ 1024 = **1.5 MB**. Convert first, then divide up the ladder.

practice.q: Which of the following is the **largest**?
practice.solution: Convert to KB: 0.5 GB = 5,24,288 KB; 1 MB = 1024 KB; 10,00,000 bytes ≈ 977 KB. **0.5 GB wins**.
practice.shortcut: Everything into one unit, then compare.

practice.q: A text file of **2 KB** contains how many **bits**?
practice.solution: 2 KB = 2048 bytes; 2048 × 8 = **16384 bits**. Two conversions: ×1024 (KB→B), then ×8 (B→bits).

practice.q: A line speed of **8 Mbps** (megabits per second) moves how much **file data** per second?
practice.solution: 8 bits = 1 byte, so 8 megabits/s = **1 megabyte/s** of file data. Line speeds are always in bits; files are in bytes.

practice.q: At a steady **16 Mbps**, downloading a **10 MB** file takes about —
practice.solution: File in bits: 10 × 8 = 80 megabits. Time = 80 ÷ 16 = **5 seconds**. Same-unit division does it in one line.

practice.q: The **smallest unit** of data in a computer is —
practice.solution: A **bit** (binary digit) — one 0 or 1 — is the smallest unit. A nibble is 4 bits and a byte is 8.

practice.q: **Word length** of a computer refers to —
options: The dictionary size of its software
The number of bits the CPU processes in one operation
The number of bytes on its disk
practice.solution: Word length = the CPU's natural chunk size — 32-bit and 64-bit processors are named by it.

practice.q: Which of the following is **NOT** a memory-size unit?
practice.solution: **Mbps** = megabits per second — a data-transfer **speed**. TB, PB and GB are size units.

practice.q: The decimal value of the binary number **(1101)₂** is —
practice.solution: 1×8 + 1×4 + 0×2 + 1×1 = **13**. Add the powers of 2 wherever a 1 appears.
practice.shortcut: Powers 8-4-2-1; add where there is a 1.

practice.q: The hexadecimal number **(1A)₁₆** equals which decimal number?
practice.solution: 1×16 + 10 = **26** (A = 10). Watch the digit order — A1 would be 161.
practice.shortcut: Left digit ×16, right digit added; A=10.

practice.q: The octal number **(67)₈** equals which decimal number?
practice.solution: 6×8 + 7 = **55**. Position values in octal are 1, 8, 64, …

practice.q: The hexadecimal number **(3E)₁₆** equals which decimal number?
practice.shortcut: E = 14; multiply the left digit by 16.

practice.q: The **binary** equivalent of decimal **45** is —
practice.solution: 45 ÷ 2 chain: remainders 1,0,1,1,0,1 read upward → **101101**. Verify: 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 45. ✔

practice.q: The decimal number **100** in **hexadecimal** is —
The decimal number **58** in **octal** is —
The decimal number **1000** in **hexadecimal** is —
practice.shortcut: Two rounds of division by 16; E = 14.

practice.q: The binary number **(1101011)₂** in **octal** is —
practice.solution: Groups of 3 from the right: 001 101 011 → **(153)₈**. Check via decimal: 107 = 1×64 + 5×8 + 3. ✔

practice.q: The binary number **(11011011)₂** in **hexadecimal** is —
practice.solution: Groups of 4 from the right: 1101 1011 → 13, 11 → **(DB)₁₆**. Check: 219 = 13×16 + 11. ✔

practice.q: How many **different values** can **8 bits** represent?
practice.solution: 2⁸ = **256** values, from 0 up to 255. 'Largest value' would be 255; 'number of values' is 256.

practice.q: Which of the following **cannot** be an **octal** number?
practice.solution: Octal uses only the digits 0–7. **789** contains 8 and 9, so it is impossible in base 8.

practice.q: Which of the following **cannot** be a **hexadecimal** number?
practice.solution: Hexadecimal digits run 0–9 and A–F. **2H4** contains H, which does not exist in base 16 (letters stop at F).
practice.shortcut: Letters stop at F — anything beyond is fake hex.

practice.q: Which of the following is an **input** device?
practice.solution: A **scanner** converts a paper document into digital data flowing **into** the computer. The other three all receive data from it.
practice.shortcut: Data in = input. Plotters, monitors, speakers push data out.

practice.q: A **joystick** is mainly used as an input device for —
practice.solution: A **joystick** feeds direction commands into the computer — the classic controller for games and flight simulators.

practice.q: In supermarkets, the device that reads the **black-and-white striped code** on products is the —
practice.solution: A **barcode reader** (or scanner) reads the striped product code and sends it to the billing system. OMR reads bubbles, MICR reads cheque ink.

practice.q: A **biometric device** that opens a laptop by reading your fingerprint works as a(n) —
practice.solution: The fingerprint scanner feeds your biometric data **into** the system — an input device (same family as iris and face readers).
practice.shortcut: It reads you, then the computer checks — data flows in.

practice.q: Which of the following is an **output** device?
practice.solution: The **monitor** displays processed results — output. Keyboard, microphone and scanner all send data in.

practice.q: Output on a **monitor** (seen but not printed) is called a —
practice.solution: **Soft copy** = screen output, temporary and intangible. Paper output is a hard copy.

practice.q: **Large engineering drawings and maps** are best printed on a —
practice.solution: A **plotter** draws continuous large-format lines — the standard output device for CAD drawings, maps and posters.
practice.shortcut: Big drawings need a plotter's pen arm.

practice.q: Which of the following is **NOT** an input device?
practice.solution: The **printer** produces output. Keyboard, mouse and microphone are all input devices.
practice.shortcut: Three inputs and one output — spot the odd direction.

practice.q: Which device serves as **both** input and output?
practice.solution: A **touch screen** takes your taps as input and shows results as output — both roles in one panel.
practice.shortcut: You touch it (in) and read it (out).

practice.q: A **headset** used for a video call contains which input–output pair?
practice.solution: The **mic sends your voice in** (input); the **speakers bring the other voice out** (output) — one device, both directions.

practice.q: Which of the following is an **impact** printer?
practice.solution: **Dot matrix** pins strike an inked ribbon against the paper — the definition of impact printing. Laser and inkjet never hit the paper.

practice.q: **OCR** technology is used to —
options: Read pencil bubbles on answer sheets
Convert scanned/printed characters into editable text
practice.solution: **OCR = Optical Character Recognition** — it turns an image of printed or handwritten characters into real editable text. Bubbles = OMR; cheque ink = MICR.

practice.q: A **3D printer** differs from ordinary printers because it —
options: Builds a physical solid object layer by layer
practice.solution: A **3D printer** is an output device that adds material layer after layer to create a real solid model — no paper involved.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. Dot matrix is an impact printer.
2. Laser printer is a non-impact printer.
3. A plotter is mainly used for printing text documents.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Statements 1 and 2 are the standard printer classification. Statement 3 is wrong — plotters are for **large drawings, maps and CAD**, not text.

practice.q: A **parallel** port transfers data —
options: Eight bits (a byte) at a time
Only in one direction, never back
practice.solution: A parallel port lays **8 wires side by side** and moves a whole byte per transfer — the old printer (LPT) port.

practice.q: Which port was traditionally used to connect **printers** (the LPT port)?
practice.solution: The 25-pin **parallel (LPT)** port was the standard printer connection before USB took over.

practice.q: **Serial** ports suit slow data over long distances mainly because they —
options: Need fewer wires, so the signal stays stable over long cables
practice.solution: Sending **one bit after another** needs only a few conductors — cheaper, less interference, reliable across long cables. Parallel's many wires limit it to short runs.

practice.q: Which port carries **digital video and audio** to a TV through a **single cable**?
practice.solution: **HDMI** (High-Definition Multimedia Interface) sends picture and sound together in one digital cable.
practice.shortcut: HDMI = Home theatre: both signals, one wire.

practice.q: The **RJ-45** socket on a computer is used for —
practice.solution: **RJ-45** is the Ethernet port — the tabbed socket that accepts the LAN cable.

practice.q: The round **6-pin PS/2** ports on older PCs were used for —
practice.solution: **PS/2** was the dedicated pair of round ports for the keyboard (purple) and mouse (green) before USB replaced them.
practice.shortcut: PS/2 = the two round holes at the back.

practice.q: The **green 3.5 mm socket** at the back of a desktop PC is for —
practice.solution: On the standard colour code, **green = audio out** (speakers/headphones), pink = microphone, blue = line-in.

practice.q: **Hot-swappable** means a device can be —
options: Connected or removed while the computer is running
Used only when the PC is switched off
practice.solution: **Hot-swap = plug or unplug with the system running** — no restart. USB is the everyday example.

practice.q: A **pen drive works without its own battery** because —
options: The USB port supplies power (5 V) along with data
practice.solution: USB carries **both data and power** — about 5 volts — so bus-powered devices like pen drives and small keyboards need no adapter.
practice.shortcut: One cable, two jobs: data + power.

practice.q:
Consider the statements about **USB**:
1. It is hot-swappable.
2. It supplies electrical power to connected devices.
3. It sends data as a serial stream.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: All three define USB: hot-swappable, bus-powered (5 V), and **serial** (the S in USB — Universal Serial Bus, one bit at a time).
practice.shortcut: The full form itself confirms statement 3.

practice.q: Which port carries **video only** and **no audio**?
practice.solution: **VGA** is the analog video-only standard — the 15-pin blue connector. HDMI and DisplayPort carry audio too.
practice.shortcut: VGA = Video Graphics Array — video's in the name.

practice.q: Which statement comparing **VGA and HDMI** is correct?
options: VGA is digital and HDMI is analog
VGA is analog video-only; HDMI is digital audio + video
practice.solution: VGA = old analog, picture only. HDMI = modern digital, picture **and** sound in one cable — that is why one HDMI wire replaces a VGA plus an audio cable.
practice.shortcut: The cable count proves the exam line.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. A serial port sends one bit at a time.
2. The parallel (LPT) port was traditionally used for printers.
3. A VGA cable carries stereo audio.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Statements 1 and 2 are the serial/parallel classics. Statement 3 is wrong — **VGA is video-only**; audio needs a separate cable.
practice.shortcut: VGA never carries sound — the standing trap.

practice.q: The storage capacity of a standard **CD-ROM** is about —
practice.solution: A standard CD holds about **700 MB**. 4.7 GB is a single-layer DVD, 25 GB a single-layer Blu-ray, and 1.44 MB was the old floppy.

practice.q: A **single-layer DVD** stores approximately —
practice.solution: **4.7 GB** per layer — about seven CDs' worth. Dual-layer DVDs reach roughly 8.5 GB.

practice.q: Which disc uses a **blue-violet laser**, letting it store far more data than a DVD?
practice.solution: **Blu-ray**'s blue-violet laser has a shorter wavelength, so pits can be packed tighter — 25 GB on a single layer (hence the name 'Blu-ray').

practice.q: Arrange by **increasing capacity** (single layer): A. DVD  B. CD  C. Blu-ray
practice.solution: CD (700 MB) < DVD (4.7 GB) < Blu-ray (25 GB) — **B, A, C**.

practice.q: A **dual-layer DVD** stores roughly —
practice.solution: Two layers of about 4.7 GB and 3.8 GB give a dual-layer DVD roughly **8.5 GB** — nearly double the single-layer figure.

practice.q: Which storage device has **no moving parts**?
practice.solution: An **SSD** is pure flash chips — nothing spins or seeks. HDDs, DVD drives and tapes are all mechanical.

practice.q: A **pen drive** stores data on —
practice.solution: Pen drives (and memory cards, SSDs) use **flash memory** — non-volatile chips that keep data without power.
practice.shortcut: Pen drive = flash in your pocket.

practice.q: A traditional **hard disk (HDD)** stores data on —
practice.solution: The HDD's arms read and write **magnetic patterns on spinning platters** — a mechanical, cheaper-per-GB design.
practice.shortcut: Hard disk = hard platters that spin.

practice.q: Which is a reason an **HDD** is still preferred over an SSD in some systems?
options: It is cheaper per GB for large capacities
practice.solution: HDDs lose on speed and shock-resistance but win clearly on **cost per terabyte** — the reason bulk storage still ships on spinning disks.
practice.shortcut: Speed buys SSD; bulk buys HDD.

practice.q: Banks and research labs archive huge volumes on **magnetic tape** because it is —
options: Very cheap per TB and durable for long-term storage
practice.solution: Tape wins on **cost and longevity**, not speed — perfect for archives that are rarely read.
practice.shortcut: Archive on tape; work on disk.

practice.q: Keeping backup copies of files on **internet servers** so they are reachable anywhere is called —
practice.solution: **Cloud backup** copies your data to remote servers over the internet — accessible from any device with a login.

practice.q: Which storage medium gives **random (direct) access**?
practice.solution: A hard disk's heads jump straight to any track — **random access**. Tape must be wound through everything in between — sequential.

practice.q: Which of the following is **NOT** an optical storage medium?
practice.solution: A **pen drive** is flash storage — no laser, no pits. CD, DVD and Blu-ray are all read optically.
practice.shortcut: Laser family: CD-DVD-BD. Flash family: pen drive, card, SSD.

practice.q:
Match the medium to its technology:
A. HDD  B. Blu-ray  C. Pen drive  D. LTO tape
options: A-magnetic platters, B-optical laser, C-flash chips, D-magnetic tape
A-flash chips, B-magnetic platters, C-optical laser, D-magnetic tape
A-magnetic tape, B-flash chips, C-optical laser, D-magnetic platters
A-magnetic platters, B-optical laser, C-magnetic tape, D-flash chips
practice.solution: HDD spins magnetised platters; Blu-ray is read by a blue-violet laser; the pen drive is flash chips; LTO is archival magnetic tape — one example of each family.

practice.q:
Consider the statements:
1. SSDs are more shock-resistant than HDDs.
2. HDDs store data magnetically.
3. Flash memory loses its data as soon as power is cut.
Which are correct?
practice.solution: Statements 1 and 2 are standard. Statement 3 is wrong — **flash is non-volatile**; it keeps data without power (that is the whole point of a pen drive).
